implementation_notes: Filtering is a stdlib extension on every collection: `list.filter { it.header("type") == "price" }` returns only the matching elements, with `filterNot` for the inverse and `filterKeys`/`filterValues` for the map cases; the predicate is inlined but the result is an eager copy, so large or unbounded message feeds switch to `Sequence`/`asSequence()`. A MessageFilter class earns its place only when criteria are injected as configuration (`(Message) -> Boolean`) or must be named, observable components.
pitfalls: filter on Iterable is eager and copies the accepted elements; Sequence/Flow is required for large or unbounded feeds.
The predicate must stay side-effect free: with Sequence/Flow it is evaluated lazily and may run again per element in composed pipelines.
Kotlin has type-specific overloads (Map.filter keeps a Map, Array.filter returns a List); mixing them up silently changes the collection type.

variants.name: Flow operator for message streams
variants.implementation_notes: For messages arriving asynchronously, `Flow<T>.filter` is the streaming realization: a suspend operator applied per emitted value with back-pressure semantics, so non-matching values are dropped before the collector's code runs. The predicate is `suspend (T) -> Boolean`, which may consult a repository or tenant service without blocking a thread, and `filterNot` covers the discard side. Use Flow when the filter sits in a pipeline (buffer/debounce/merge); keep the collections filter for materialised batches.
pitfalls: A blocking call inside the predicate stalls the collecting coroutine and its dispatcher thread; use suspend APIs or withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
Flow is cold: every collector re-runs the predicate, so a filter with side effects executes once per collector.
The predicate must not swallow CancellationException, or structured concurrency stops working for the whole pipeline.
